title: How to Build Durable Agentic Systems with Google Antigravity: From Instructions to Loops
raw_text:
I watched the discussion on agentic loops grow louder over the past few months. But for me, the reality is simpler: prompt engineering has shifted from individual tasks to systems design, and the harness around the model (not the model itself) is now my primary constraint in software engineering. In this article, I'll show you how to build and verify those harnesses so you can move from single-turn instructions to durable agentic loops in Google Antigravity . Not all tasks are equal You can categorize the work that we give to our agents into five distinct tiers, scaling from a quick question up through Agile tasks, stories, and epics to a continuous system: A simple question : This does not require an agent; an assistant can answer it. A task / idea: This is one where a single prompt can zero-shot it. Use Google AI Studio to quickly transform ideas to functional prototypes. An app / larger feature / story: The kind of work that required weekly planning and splitting into subtasks before AI. Use loops for execution and full-featured agents, like Google Antigravity. This tier is also where your steering moves upstream: You lock in the spec, the plan, and the executable tests before any loop runs. A project / epic: A few features that make a cohesive story when connected. Loops here might help with planning too. This is also where one needs to go beyond simple turn-based prompting. A system : An overview of all of the projects and tasks. This is where you write AGENTS.md project instructions, create skills , set up sidecars , wire up verification gates, and configure an instrument cluster to keep themselves on top of everything. Loops at this level make the biggest difference and come with similarly higher risks. Figure 1: Five tiers of engineering work, from single prompts to verified agentic loops. Why the loop? The baseline of software development is shifting. This shift represents a basic law of human nature: we seek the highest leverage possible, moving from manual labor to delegation, and finally to orchestration. Because attention is the new bottleneck, anything that lets the work continue with less interruption could make a move in the right direction. By early 2026, empirical research of open-source projects estimated that coding agent adoption had reached between 22% and 29% of more than 128,000 active repositories on GitHub. Those who become proficient in agentic workflows now operate with a level of leverage that elevates their entire team's productivity. However, it also increases the cognitive load on everyone who is taking responsibility at the systemic level. To understand this shift, let's trace the technical lineage of loops and set some high level expectations. Academic foundations The academic seed was Yao et al.'s ReAct paper in October 2022, which interleaved reasoning traces with tool calls. ReAct beat reinforcement learning baselines by 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop by reasoning before acting, mirroring human nature: we perform better when verbalizing plans. Then came AutoGPT in early 2023, raising millions in venture funding. While early iterations of ReAct frequently spun in infinite loops, it proved developers wanted hands-off automation, highlighting the need for structural guardrails. Stateless experimentation In mid-2025, developers ran stateless bash loops that piped prompts into command-line agents and reset context files on every tick. Resetting context prevents cognitive bloat and acknowledges that human memory limits also apply to models. Stateless bash loops worked only because the durable state lived outside the model: in Git history, in progress files, and in the test suite. It successfully built self-hosting compilers over months of automated runs. By spring 2026, major tool environments absorbed this pattern, shipping native commands like /goal to let agents run unattended loops. The mathematics of autonomy Consider a theoretical example: If you put your agent in a flat sequential chain to complete multiple tasks in a row, the agent's success rate degrades exponentially. When each of its individual steps operates as an independent probability event, a sequence of N steps has a cumulative success rate of p N . For instance, if you run a task requiring 20 consecutive file modifications with a model that has p = 0.95 accuracy, then you face a success rate of only 36% . Without your structural interventions, they will fail almost certainly. Is 0.95 a real number? Treat it as an illustrative per-step reliability, not as a benchmark result. Even a frontier model reaches reliable multi-step outcomes only when it runs inside a verified harness. If your own per-step reliability sits closer to 75%, then the raw chain is already under 6% by step 10. The verification around the model sets the ceiling, which is why the loop matters. This is why you need evaluation loops. A verification gate should not force your agent to retry indefinitely (which causes infinite spinning runaways). Instead, it should pinpoint where the error occurred and allow the model exactly one targeted retry to fix it. If your agent has a 95% base accuracy, and your evaluation loop has a 95% chance of spotting and fixing the error on that single retry, the effective step success probability rises to 0.95 + (0.05 x 0.95) = 99.75% . That arithmetic assumes the check is independent of the worker, so the gate has to be an outside check. Compilers, test suites, and linters give you that for free, and behavioral evaluations let you assert on discrete tool calls and intermediate actions in seconds instead of waiting on a full end-to-end benchmark. For semantic judgments that a deterministic test cannot make, I pair models from different families so the reviewer does not share the worker's blind spot. Even if fixing fails, just spotting the error with a 95% accuracy, lets you jump in and manually realign the system while keeping the same 99.75% subagent accuracy and only paying the cost of human-in-the-loop intervention. The table below shows the probability of completion across different chain lengths, comparing raw models to this single-retry course-correction topology: Chain Length 95% Accuracy 95% x 95% Loop 3 Steps 86% 99% 5 Steps 77% 99% 10 Steps 60% 98% 15 Steps 46% 96% 20 Steps 36% 95% 30 Steps 21% 93% 50 Steps 8% 88% What about context bloat? If each step in a chain adds approximately 1% of context in tokens, you end up with a chain that is not much longer than 50 steps before we require compression. A 95% base accuracy that can be evaluated (and course corrected with 95% accuracy for each dimension that we care about) should keep you at good success rates for such individual running agents. If you establish a scalable way to divide and conquer problems, you can apply similar principles to drive your subagents. As we can see, at 20 steps, a 95% accuracy paired with a single-retry corrective loop yields a 95% end-to-end success rate (assuming the correction itself stays under our 20 steps soft limit) while keeping context size reasonable. Note that there is no explicit requirement for the correction to be AI or human driven, but rather it needs to produce accurate and verifiable results. This is where you divide problems into tasks that require a small number of steps each. If a problem is more complex, it remains approachable, but it must be divided into smaller subproblems, and so on. For our example, this means allocating up to 20 steps for each level agent, task, and trajectory and another 20 steps for the next level supervisory agent to consolidate contributions. To prevent drift, establish separate evaluations at all subagent and supervisory levels with a final acceptance criteria. Lastly, you must evaluate these metrics at least once for each level to verify that they measure the right target before running automation at a higher level. These are general estimations, but help you quickly decide whether you should split a problem, repeat a step, or commit results and move on. In practice, your numbers will look different, but the scaling laws will be similar. How to build a durable system What started as a source of friction has now become one of my primary driving curiosities: how do we build automation when we still have a lot to learn about the craft itself? I have a few ideas. To build a loop that does not run off a cliff, you must establish core guardrails that will keep accuracy high and will allow us to debug and intervene whenever necessary. Specifically, these are the pillars I identified: Durable state : Git-backed checkpoints ensure that your agent can resume work after a crash. Verification gates : Automated test suites and compilers deterministically check that the changes are correct. Write the acceptance criteria and the tests upstream, before implementation starts, and make one rule explicit in your project instructions: an agent cannot pass a gate by deleting or weakening a test. When done properly, gates can have >95% accuracy. However, you should be on the lookout for edge cases you might have forgotten about. Especially if verification, evaluation, or manual validation success rates diverge for any of your features. Evals : Anything that cannot be deterministically verified but is important should have an evaluation or benchmark which you can later inspect for accuracy. Try to write them in a way that will keep answers to a simple yes or no and accuracy high, ideally over 95%. If you're getting results that point to confusion or unexpected failures, you probably need to split the criteria into simpler ones. Halt conditions : Turn limits (as we saw above, 20 seems to be the sweet spot) and token or dollar cost ceilings stop runs before API budgets get out of control. Standardized skills and instructions : Reusable utilities, documented in the SKILL.md format, preferably bundled with code and source of truth references. Pair them with an AGENTS.md that holds the project invariants every run load. Skills stay on disk until their description matches the task, so they do not eat into the 20-step context window. These pillars don't name a model version, but rather a model family. Individual model leads last only weeks. The asset that survives each release is the harness and its processes: the AGENTS.md instructions every run loads, the SKILL.md modules loaded only when relevant, the isolated Cloud Run sandbox where the loop runs around the clock, the deterministic checks, and the cross-model review. When a run fails or you have to intervene, patch your harness along with the code: a new test, a line in AGENTS.md , a note in the skill. The next run inherits the lesson even though its context starts from zero. Platform built-in systems Platforms like Google Antigravity have codified these patterns ( /grill-me and /goal ) into built-in primitives, shifting the work from custom scripts to platform capabilities for most straightforward use cases. The same harness files travel with the repository whether you run Google Antigravity 2.0, the agy CLI, or Antigravity inside VS Code, JetBrains, or Cursor. I would encourage you to give these a try. Do remember, however, to keep an eye on trajectory lengths and look for model confusion. I myself frequently rely on the /goal primitives in Google Antigravity 2.0 when coordinating multi-turn tasks that require extensive validation and measurements before completion. To anchor this execution, use the /grill-me command for an interactive interview to lock in design constraints, invariants, and the tests that decide success before running /goal loops. Constructing the metrics for this technical article and then editing it is just one example of how I use these execution loops. By pairing /goal with /grill-me , you can establish an effective pair-programming dynamic: alignment on intent, followed by autonomy in execution. Custom DIY loops To understand the evolution of loops, compare two distinct architectures for DIY agentic loops: Stateless five-liner Geoffrey Huntley's "Ralph" loop is a prime example of stateless architecture. A good agent skill could fix much of this limitation by instructing the model to output relevant progress reports in wiki-like markdown files and track changes by looking at git logs. Still, this complexity has led to developer challenges in larger multi-agent environments, for which custom loops seem to hold the promise. So what if you want to go to the deep end? If you want to write a custom loop from scratch, here is a practical Python implementation using the Google Antigravity SDK . Specifically, this loop does the following actions: Initializes a supervisor session. Executes a task. Verifies the output with the real test suite. Feeds the actual failure output back for exactly one targeted retry. Enforces strict call and token budgets. Not every task inside it is equal, so neither is the model. The supervisor and the implementer run on Gemini 4 Carbon because orchestration, architecture, and the complex fixes need frontier reasoning, codebase search goes to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and verification goes to a deterministic script that costs no tokens at all. The Guide to AI Tokenomics covers the budgeting side of this split. import subprocess

from google.antigravity import Agent, LocalAgentConfig, types
from google.antigravity.hooks import policy

 """Verification gate: run the test suite and keep the real failure output."""

 ["go", "test", "./..."], cwd=workspace_path, capture_output=True, text=True
 )

researcher = types.SubagentConfig(

feature_implementer = types.SubagentConfig(
 name="feature_implementer",

 ),

 capabilities=types.SubagentCapabilities(

 types.BuiltinTools.VIEW_FILE,
 types.BuiltinTools.EDIT_FILE,
 types.BuiltinTools.CREATE_FILE,

 await response.text() # Drain the stream before reading the stop reason

 types.StopReason.MAX_MODEL_CALLS_EXCEEDED,
 types.StopReason.MAX_TOTAL_TOKENS_EXCEEDED,

 print(f"Loop halted: budget exceeded ({response.stop_reason}).")

 print(f"Tokens used so far: {usage.total_token_count or 0:,} / 200,000")

If the verification still fails after that, the loop returns False and a human takes the seat instead of the model spinning until the budget runs out. If you prefer not to build and host your own custom SDK loops from scratch, use Antigravity Agent , an autonomous, asynchronous coding agent. Antigravity Agent operates in a secure, isolated Google Cloud sandbox. This way you can create similar agentic loops by using managed agents to orchestrate execution plans under Google managed infrastructure. Alternatively, you can run the preceding loop inside a long-lived Cloud Run sandbox so that the loop keeps working after you close your laptop. No one size fits all You must establish a clear boundary for each of your validation systems that lets you stay in control. No matter how perfect your loop, if you , as the responsible human, cannot sign off on your agent's output, there is minimal value in any of the artifacts it is producing. The good news is that building a quality evaluation scorecard or a loop algorithm uses a similar process to producing any other type of software artifact. So, much of the execution will be automated. Finally, to make a sound judgment, you should observe each loop from the inside. As you see things working out, with this acquired confidence you step one level up. This is the only way to learn where the agent struggles and how to improve the process itself.

title: The visual evolution of Looker: Modern design for enterprise data storytelling
raw_text: Over the past year, we’ve focused on making Looker easier to use for every business user. We started by redesigning the exploration experience with drag-and-drop workspaces , streamlined field pickers, and conversational analytics to make it easier to start from a blank canvas. The next step is elevating how your data is seen and interpreted. This November, we are rolling out a major update for Looker’s visual language that brings new native chart types and dashboard controls to your dashboards, Explores, and feeds into your generative Data Apps . Everything runs on Looker's governed semantic foundation and context from Knowledge Catalog . Here's what's new: See the state of the business at a glance KPI visualizations: Display core metrics with explicit period-over-period delta indicators, percentage trends, and directional status at a glance. Displaying core business metrics and period-over-period trends with a KPI visualization. Bullet charts and gauges: Stack actual performance against targets, quotas, and qualitative threshold bands in space-efficient layouts. Tracking actual performance against targets with a Radial gauge chart. Compact numbers: Automatically render high-volume numbers into clean, human-readable formats ($2.4M instead of $2,400,000) that stay readable across any screen size. Showcase the data behind the numbers Sankey diagrams: Map multi-stage conversion funnels, user drop-offs, budget allocations, and material flows with native Sankey diagrams. Mapping multi-stage conversion flows with a native Sankey diagram. Hierarchical tables: Drill into multi-level, nested data trees (such as category rollups or departmental cost centers) within a single structured tabular view. Drilling into multi-level nested data within a Hierarchical table. Histograms: Plot frequency distributions and spot data skew and outliers across numeric variables without writing table calculations. Plotting frequency distributions and outliers across numeric variables with a Histogram. Network charts: Visualize interdependencies, entity relationships, and interconnected graph nodes to uncover clusters and bottlenecks. Visualizing entity relationships, clusters, and bottlenecks with a Network chart. Modernized dashboards and in-context controls Keep stakeholders engaged with a boardroom-ready design and faster, more focused interactivity: A modernized dashboard: More modern typography, refined spacing, cleaner table padding, and upgraded palettes give every dashboard a contemporary, polished look right out of the box. Filters on visualizations (Preview): Apply and adjust filters directly on individual dashboard tiles, so viewers can isolate specific cuts of data without reloading the entire page. Applying and adjusting chart-level filters directly on a modernized Looker dashboard tile. Agent-assisted custom visualizations Several of the new charts in this release started as custom visualization plugins in the Looker Marketplace . Because they are now supported natively in Looker, we are retiring the associated plugins from the Marketplace. Existing dashboards that use those Marketplace plugins will continue to work. While Looker’s large native library covers most everyday analytics, every industry has specialized visualization requirements. A chipmaker may need to plot defect density across a silicon wafer map, a logistics team may want to overlay warehouse floor plans onto live shipping metrics, and a finance team might ask for a multi-step variance bridge that follows internal accounting rules. These cases come up often. Previously, building one of these custom charts against Looker's Visualization API meant either writing JavaScript yourself or waiting for a front-end developer to help. Looker's agentic BI changes that. To support these domain-specific builds, we are launching a new custom visualization skill in the open-source looker-skills repository . This skill lets you use your AI coding agent of choice, such as Antigravity, Claude or Codex, to develop, test, iterate, and deploy your own custom visualizations. Describe the chart in natural language, and the agent writes the code against Looker's Visualization API. You can refine the design conversationally until the chart looks right, and then have the agent deploy it for you. Sunburst, KPI radar, and calendar heatmap charts generated with the Looker custom visualization skill. Nobody on your team needs to know JavaScript. Still, if you prefer a specific JavaScript library, you can ask for D3, Vega-Lite, ECharts, Chart.js, or React, or have the agent draw the chart from scratch in SVG. Whatever approach you pick, the chart receives the underlying data from your LookML model and inherits native drill menus, cross-filtering, and dashboard controls alongside your standard tiles. This same visual system and agent-driven workflow also powers Looker Data Apps ( in preview). When your use case grows beyond a single custom chart tile into a multi-step operational workflow, you can use your AI agent to assemble a full data app that shares Looker's modernized typography, palettes, and governed LookML metrics. Whether you’re adding a bespoke chart to an existing dashboard or building a standalone application, every view stays consistent and grounded in the same semantic model. Getting started Explore the new native visualizations and modernized dashboard controls in your Looker environment today, or visit the Looker documentation to learn more. Try the custom visualization skill in your own Looker project by visiting the open-source looker-skills repository on GitHub.

title: COLD RELIC: A Case Study in Impersonation and Compromise
raw_text: Written by: Josh Murchie, John Wolfram, Joseph Spero, Peter Ukhanov, Fernando Tomlinson, Jr., Wesley Shields Introduction Over the past year, Mandiant has responded to a series of linked intrusions demonstrating how Russian cyber espionage group COLD RELIC (formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057; also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) turns a single cloud compromise into a springboard for ongoing third party compromise and espionage. Most recently, Mandiant investigated a 2026 compromise at a US-based organization where COLD RELIC directly weaponized data, the corporate staff directory, and identities stolen during a late-2025 compromise, which Mandiant also investigated, at a separate US-based organization. COLD RELIC is a Russian state-sponsored threat group that the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has assessed operates within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). The group is known for implementing sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns with the aim to gain access to information of strategic or political relevance to the Russian government, as well as to leverage compromised access to target compromised individuals’ broader social and professional networks. Once COLD RELIC compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets. While COLD RELIC has largely maintained a low profile, yielding minimal public reporting relative to other Russia-nexus threat actors, it has been highly successful at compromising high-value targets (including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America) while maintaining a consistent operational tempo. While Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has tracked and disrupted COLD RELIC phishing campaigns since 2015, recent Mandiant incident response investigations have uncovered critical new insights into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft. We are sharing this end-to-end analysis—along with actionable detection and hardening guidance—to help organizations defend against COLD RELIC’s ongoing use of stolen pretexts, localized residential proxies, and cross-cloud identity abuse. As part of our efforts to thwart this threat actor, we issue Government-backed attack alerts when we detect COLD RELIC targeting Google accounts. COLD RELIC remains an active threat; GTIG has observed evidence of new phishing operations as recently as November 2026. Threat Detail Over more than a decade of tracking COLD RELIC alongside Mandiant incident response investigations, we have observed the group continually refine how it leverages data harvested from one intrusion to enable follow-on operations against downstream targets. In late 2025, COLD RELIC downloaded a large volume of data from a US-based organization, searching for names, email addresses, and email archives, likely to fulfill broader intelligence requirements. In 2026, Mandiant investigated a subsequent COLD RELIC intrusion at a second US-based organization where phishing URL parameters and impersonation pretexts indicated that COLD RELIC likely leveraged contact and relationship context from the first organization to target the second. One of the hallmarks of COLD RELIC phishing campaigns is the use of a compromised website as the initial link that will redirect the target to the actual phishing domain. This provides COLD RELIC with a layer of misdirection and hides their phishing domains, while also giving them a chance to fingerprint anyone visiting the link to determine if they should be redirected or not. A COLD RELIC phishing link usually contains a parameter on the end of it with a value that is set by the attacker and often indicates a relationship to a previous victim or what the lure is. For example, a URL might look like these (though this is not always the case): https://compromised.example.com/some_path/some_file.php?file=<previous_victim_name> https://compromised.example.com/some_path/some_file.php?ref=<lure_name> Figure 1: Sample URLs incorporating targeted individuals’ names or lure topics During Mandiant’s incident response investigation at the second US-based organization, responders identified that COLD RELIC initiated contact over an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee from the first victim organization. In parallel, GTIG correlated a COLD RELIC redirector URL from the intrusion that had been submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026, whose query parameter referenced the first victim organization. Case Study 1 - Stolen Credentials to Data Exfiltration During the late-2025 intrusion, GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise the cloud productivity environment of a US-based organization. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC leveraged a residential proxy network in the US located in close geographical proximity to the victim. COLD RELIC authenticated using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account, in combination with a multi-factor authentication ( MFA) push notification fatigue attack. After the victim user accepted an MFA request, COLD RELIC registered a device model previously unseen within the tenant of the victim organization. COLD RELIC leveraged passkeys, MFA backup codes, and rogue MFA devices to retain access throughout the intrusion. COLD RELIC used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization’s cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a COLD RELIC-operated email account and downloading files directly. While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, COLD RELIC accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion. COLD RELIC also exported full employee lists and initiated a domain-wide data export via Google Workspace Customer Takeout using Super Admin privileges. Unlike individual end-user Google Takeout, Customer Takeout is an administrative tenant-wide export tool; these requests are logged in Google Workspace Admin audit logs ( CUSTOMER_TAKEOUT_CREATED ), and administrators can also disable Google Takeout for users at the organizational level . Following mass data theft and antiforensics activities, COLD RELIC maintained access to the victim organization for several months and performed additional activities including: Email inbox sync via OAuth to external email clients Reauthentication using unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys that persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls Targeted cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information, and other documents relevant to COLD RELIC’s intelligence collection requirements When the threat actor was removed from the victim organization’s infrastructure, GTIG observed COLD RELIC leveraging email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization. These impersonated accounts were used to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles with renewed social engineering attempts. Case Study 2 - Leveraging Previous Compromise - Initial Approach During the second intrusion, COLD RELIC demonstrated competency in navigating multi-cloud environments and federated authentication mechanisms. GTIG observed COLD RELIC operators compromise a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a US-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace. To gain initial access, COLD RELIC impersonated an employee of the organization impacted in Case Study 1 to establish a pretext for communications over a secure messaging app. The threat actor ultimately shared phishing links during the course of the conversation. These phishing links, designed to steal credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID, redirected the victim to document lures relevant to the ongoing conversation in order to avoid raising suspicion. Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, COLD RELIC registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion. A redacted and abbreviated version of the social engineering conversation is included below (image generated with LLMs): Figure 2: Redacted, LLM-generated depiction of observed threat actor social engineering engagement By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, COLD RELIC increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, COLD RELIC was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive. Post-Compromise Activity After gaining initial access to an organization, COLD RELIC registers rogue MFA devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence. Once persistence is secured, COLD RELIC conducts aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations, accessing email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. While COLD RELIC's primary objective post-compromise is mass collection and download of files and email archives, it simultaneously performs targeted queries for specific terms of interest. In particular, COLD RELIC searches for credentials, personnel information, email archives (.pst files), and documents related to their collection requirements. Additionally, COLD RELIC seeks out data that can support subsequent spear-phishing operations, including organizational rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules to build convincing pretexts for future targets. Beyond seeking out data to support subsequent operations, COLD RELIC also appeared to repurpose the account used in Case Study 2 for follow on targeting. After the compromise, the encrypted messaging application used for the initial approach recorded that the threat actor changed their profile name to a completely new person. GTIG believes this new persona was likely used to continue to target other organizations in the same professional circles in a similar manner to both of the cases documented here. Outlook and Implications COLD RELIC’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners. Their ability to navigate across multiple cloud ecosystems highlights that organizations must defend their entire identity estate holistically. GTIG will continue to track, disrupt, and expose COLD RELIC infrastructure to protect global cloud users. Remediation and Hardening As previously mentioned, GTIG has observed COLD RELIC heavily rely on residential proxy networks in the course of their intrusions. Moreover, the group goes one step further in obfuscating their activities by selecting proxies that geolocate to the same approximate location as their victim users, thereby avoiding impossible travel or other heuristic-based alerting mechanisms. GTIG recommends enriching authentication logs with residential proxy and VPN IP reputation feeds, alerting on sudden residential ASN shifts for privileged accounts, and applying conditional access policies to block or detect logons from known proxy networks. In some cases, the severity and scope of COLD RELIC intrusions were amplified due to users storing credentials and other secrets within their organization’s cloud storage platforms. This enabled COLD RELIC to pivot to additional accounts or services that it would not have otherwise been able to access, including users’ personal accounts which are typically unmonitored by their employers. Organizations can implement cloud storage Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies, such as Google Workspace’s Security & Data Protection , to warn or block users attempting to create, upload, or externally share files matching sensitive patterns. In at least one case, GTIG observed that a victim organization identified the intrusion and attempted to remediate COLD RELIC’s access to their cloud tenant via password resets for impacted accounts. However, because the threat actor hijacked sessions and the victim organization failed to also revoke all existing sessions for the accounts in question, COLD RELIC maintained access. In similar circumstances, such as Business Email Compromise (BEC) intrusions, GTIG recommends organizations revoke all user sessions in addition to forcing password resets for impacted accounts. Organizations should implement the following recommendations: Identity & Multi-Factor Authentication Enforce Phishing-Resistant MFA (FIDO2 / WebAuthn): Replace SMS, voice, and push notifications with hardware security keys (e.g., Titan Security Keys). Hardware keys are bound to the origin URL and cannot be intercepted by AiTM reverse proxies or approved via fatigue attacks. Restrict and Audit Passkey Registrations: Monitor identity logs for passkey registrations and rogue device enrollments, particularly on administrative accounts. Harden MFA Registration: Require existing administrators or out-of-band identity verification to approve new MFA devices or secondary authenticators (such as Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys). Organizations and individuals may consider enrolling in the Advanced Protection Program . Session Management & Incident Response Mandate Session & OAuth Revocation in BEC Playbooks: When remediating suspected account compromise, password changes alone are insufficient. Administrators must immediately revoke all active browser sessions, refresh tokens, and authorized third-party OAuth app permissions across both Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID, and remove any unauthorized passkeys, backup codes, or MFA devices. Audit Third-Party OAuth Grants: Continuously review authorized third-party applications in Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, flagging unexpected native desktop email clients (e.g., Thunderbird) or external mail services (e.g., Proton Mail). Network & Infrastructure Controls Detect & Block Residential Proxy Logons: Restrict administrative access from consumer ISPs, VPNs, and known residential proxy ASN ranges (e.g., AS5650, AS20115). title: Building Sovereign AI in Europe, With Europe: Our New Startup Accelerator
raw_text: Today we’re announcing an open call for applications for the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI . Available in Europe and Israel, this initiative supports startups that are building cutting-edge AI solutions for European regulatory environments. Artificial intelligence represents an estimated €1.2 trillion economic opportunity for Europe . To realize this potential, European enterprises and public institutions need to adopt advanced AI while also meeting crucial data governance requirements, including the EU AI Act , NIS2 , DORA , and national frameworks such as SecNumCloud and BSI's cloud security and sovereignty principles . We want ambitious founders to build in Europe, with solutions made in Europe. For startups, digital sovereignty cannot mean settling for second-rate tools or getting locked into a single rigid stack. It means co-engineering with Europe's tech ecosystem so founders can scale on their own terms from day one: for instance combining frontier Gemini models, open-weight models like Gemma and Mistral, and verifiable data residency and cryptographic controls delivered with local European sovereign partners. How it works This equity-free, 15-week hybrid program includes virtual and in-person sessions connecting founders with Google engineers, regulatory experts, and local partners. Selected startups receive hands-on architectural mentorship, 1:1 pairing with Google Cloud engineers, and advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act Regulatory Sandboxes. Participants will gain direct support to deploy across Google Cloud’s tiered sovereign portfolio: Sovereign cloud infrastructure : From regional data controls and external key management (data boundary) to partner-operated clouds (such as S3NS in France and Thales in Germany) and fully air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments. Auditable, private AI : Fine-tuning and deploying open-weight models like the Gemma family (including MedGemma) in sovereign environments for verifiable control over data and operations. Ecosystem and investors access : Direct engagement with European sovereign cloud operators, system integrators, and institutional investors to compress enterprise sales cycles. Who should apply We are selecting a small, high-touch cohort of late-seed to post Series A startups headquartered across Europe and Israel with strong traction that use AI to handle sensitive, regulated workloads. We’re specifically seeking startups focused on: Government and public service technologies including sovereign document processing, citizen service portals, municipal operations, smart utilities, and civic emergency grids (defense applications excluded). Healthcare and life sciences including clinical trial analytics, electronic health records (EHR/EHDS), diagnostic copilots, and hospital operations that meet compliance requirements for GDPR and the European Health Data Space . Regulated finance including credit risk modeling, anti-money laundering pipelines, fraud detection, credit underwriting pipelines, and claims processing. title: Sovereign AI in Europe: New ways to control your AI stack
raw_text: Today in Brussels, public sector leaders, policymakers and partners are meeting at the Sovereign AI Summit to discuss how to build the next decade of Europe's public services, healthcare, and finance with AI under European control. We're here with our European partners to help deliver it. Achieving that goal takes more than deciding where data is stored. When we talk with European organizations, we hear four common questions from them: Will choosing more control mean settling for less capable AI? Who can access our data, and can we prove to regulators that our controls work? Will the value that organizations create with AI stay in Europe? How can we keep AI running reliably? In May 2025, we introduced a portfolio of sovereign cloud offerings for customers to match their desired level of control to each workload. In February, we set out the commitments behind that portfolio, covering local investment, operational continuity, customer control over data, and open technology. Today, we’re building on these commitments. Gemini models are coming to Google Cloud Dedicated, our partner-operated cloud, expanding model choice beyond the open models already available in the model garden. We are also announcing new capabilities for cryptographic key control and compliance, and new work with European software companies and startups. Bringing Google AI across our sovereign portfolio Sovereignty is not one-size-fits-all, so Sovereign Cloud from Google offers three ways to run a workload. First, Google Cloud Data Boundary applies data residency, access, and encryption controls on our public cloud. A second option is Google Cloud Dedicated, which is operated by an independent local partner on isolated infrastructure. And finally, Google Distributed Cloud runs in a customer's own data center connected or fully air-gapped. Select Gemini models are already available in Google Cloud with a commitment to perform machine-learning processing of customer data in-region for these models, including within the EU. It is also available with Google Distributed Cloud. And with today’s announcement that Gemini is coming to Google Cloud Dedicated, organizations that require a locally operated cloud will be able to use it there too. Many teams also want open models, or models they have tuned themselves. In France, S3NS has made managed model serving and inference generally available on PREMI3NS, its cloud built on Google Cloud Dedicated. Teams can deploy open models from providers such as Mistral and Google through Model Garden, or bring their own models. S3NS operates the environment, designed so the deployed models and prompts remain within the PREMI3NS environment under S3NS's control. Keeping customers in control of access and keys For many European organizations, data access, encryption key access and services access dictate their sovereignty posture. On our public cloud, customers can already see when Google personnel access their data and why, approve or deny that access with Access Transparency , Access Approval , and Key Access Justifications . Customers who want more control can hold their encryption keys outside Google Cloud , which enables them to deny access to their data for any reason. Together, these controls help ensure the customer controls any and all access to their data. When customers hold keys outside Google Cloud, every key request has to travel to an external system, which can add latency and availability risk. Confidential External Key Management (cEKM), currently in preview, is designed to remove that trade-off: Customers, or their chosen local partner, hold and control access to the root keys outside Google Cloud, while key operations run inside a hardware-attested Confidential Computing environment designed to run with the low latency and reliability that data-intensive workloads, including AI, demand. Customers can also ask trusted local partners to hold their keys external from Google infrastructure. A new partnership with Telefónica in Spain (currently in preview) expands customer options beyond existing European partnerships France, Germany, Italy, Spain. Helping customers demonstrate compliance to regulators Auditing sovereignty controls and requirements is not only difficult, it often requires engineering effort. To help make audits smoother, we are introducing Data Boundary frameworks that map local and regional regulatory requirements to enforced, auditable controls. A framework for Switzerland is available today, and a framework for the EU's Digital Operational Resilience (DORA) Act is planned for financial services organizations. With Audit Manager , customers can start from a ready-made framework, adapt it to their own policies, and give auditors continuous, machine-readable evidence, designed to keep customer data within their designated boundary. Building with European operators, software vendors, and startups Sovereignty also depends on who operates the technology, and whether the value it creates stays local. That's why we work with European companies at every layer: those that operate the cloud, those that build software for it, and the startups that will build what comes next. Google Cloud Dedicated is designed so that the local partner controls the environment, can block software updates in exceptional circumstances, and can keep operating for up to 12 months in the unlikely scenario that its Dedicated instance connection to Google is severed. These design choices sit alongside the commitments we made in February, including that should Google receive an order from a national government to suspend or terminate the provision of Google Cloud's operations provided from any country, we will seek to limit, modify, or object to any such order using all available legal avenues. In France, PREMI3NS from S3NS has achieved SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. With Thales, we are extending Google Cloud Dedicated to Germany (currently in preview), to enable a sovereign hyperscale capability across the EU. Regulated workloads often stall because the security, identity, and monitoring tools that teams depend on are not available in a sovereign environment. More than a dozen software vendors have now validated their products on Google Cloud Dedicated, including European providers such as Memority and Tsuga. We also want to help the new companies and skills that AI is creating to take root in Europe. The new Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI is an equity-free program that gives startups in regulated sectors support from Google engineers, mentorship, and access to local cloud providers. What comes next We are continuing to build on the strategy we set in 2025: giving customers control that they can verify, a choice in how they operate in the cloud and who operates the environment, and access to advanced AI regardless of your deployment choices. We will keep bringing more of our AI platform to partner-operated and on-premises environments, extending access and key controls to more services, and adding frameworks for more regulations, together with the European partners who operate these services. To learn more, visit Sovereign Cloud from Google or talk to a sovereign specialist .

title: Beyond the compute bottleneck: Maximizing the ROI of AI accelerators with purpose-built storage
raw_text: There’s a lot more to AI infrastructure than just buying accelerators. Indeed, the infrastructure mandate for enterprise AI has shifted from acquiring accelerators to keeping them fully utilized. Next to these expensive accelerators, storage accounts for only a small sliver of total AI spend. However, having the wrong storage in place can put the rest of your committed compute capital at risk. To optimize your accelerators’ TCO, you need to keep them fully occupied. Very often, the challenge here is data I/O. If accelerators sit waiting to read or write data, you’re wasting money. Across the industry, insufficient storage throughput has become a primary impediment to AI success, starving models of the data they need. And the problem is only going to get worse. Gartner predicts enterprises will deploy over 150,000 agents in the next few years, so the I/O bottleneck and the challenge of orchestrating storage for agentic fleets will only compound. Organizations are eager to move their AI initiatives forward, but preventing idle compute requires a purpose-built approach to data I/O. With the demands of AI, standard enterprise storage — even a system optimized for fast analytics — will inevitably suffer from bottlenecks that leave compute resources twiddling their proverbial thumbs. AI is not a monolithic workload The most common architectural misstep we see is treating AI as a single, general-purpose workload. In reality, the physical movement of data transforms across the AI lifecycle, creating distinct I/O profiles based on how models consume and generate information: In model training , clusters read datasets at high throughput, but pause regularly to write checkpoints to record their state in event of a failure. When thousands of GPUs attempt to save this data in a single, simultaneous burst, standard storage architectures stall. That’s especially true of traditional cloud storage, which is engineered for durability. Writing checkpoints triggers thousands of administrative database transactions to safely record the files, bogging down the system, choking the network, and freezing the entire GPU cluster until the save is complete. Furthermore, saving the data is only one of the problems: If a server fails, slow storage turns a routine checkpoint recovery into a multi-hour delay, leaving expensive accelerators sitting completely idle. Inference , conversely, is real-time and latency-sensitive. As AI services scale to meet user demand, inference clusters constantly load and unload petabyte-scale model repositories quickly. In this case, a slow storage system can leave GPUs in a “cold start” as they wait for data. Also, many models now process context windows that exceed 100,000 tokens, filling up accelerator memory. Without a high-speed external cache to offload this context, when a user asks the next question, the accelerator must recalculate previous inputs, wasting compute on redundant operations. Industry-leading performance across object and file storage To solve these I/O challenges and keep expensive accelerators busy, organizations need compute, networking, and storage to be deeply integrated. As industry analysts have noted, enterprise customers gain a unique performance advantage because Google Cloud runs on the exact same storage foundation as Google's own consumer products. This foundation is built on Colossus—the planet-scale distributed file system powering Google Search, YouTube, and Gemini. Because this shared infrastructure supports billions of users daily, its reliability is continuously proven against the extreme traffic and hardware demands of Google's global consumer services. As a result, today, nine out of the world’s ten leading AI frontier model labs run on Google Cloud infrastructure because we deliver the throughput and performance they require to innovate. In fact, we spent the last two years co-designing our storage architecture directly with these frontier labs as well as with Google's own foundation model teams. For large-scale training on object storage, our architecture ensures workloads don’t have to wait on data, and successfully absorbs peak bandwidth demands. For real-time inference, enterprise platform companies like Salesforce AI Research leverage our architecture to serve complex agentic inference workloads with up to 40% fewer GPUs . We deliver these outcomes through two distinct, purpose-built storage solutions: Cloud Storage Rapid: For organizations that have standardized on cloud-native object storage, Cloud Storage Rapid provides Colossus scale and performance directly to accelerators, so they can use the data stored on object storage in their AI workflows. This eliminates the need to migrate data into separate, specialized storage silos to achieve the performance that AI workloads require. A single Rapid bucket pushes the boundaries of object storage, delivering up to 15 TB/s of throughput and 20 million queries per second with sub-millisecond latency. This makes it a strong fit for streaming large training datasets and recovering checkpoints without bottlenecking the network. For bursty workloads such as model loading across multiple locations, Rapid Cache acts as a read accelerator that co-locates active data directly with TPU and GPU clusters. With no code changes, Rapid Cache delivers up to 2.5 TB/s of aggregate read throughput, taking idle cold-start times from hours to minutes. Google Cloud Managed Lustre: For demanding AI and HPC workloads that need a parallel file system, there’s Google Cloud Managed Lustre . Built in partnership with DDN, Managed Lustre provides up to 10 TB/s of throughput per instance, absorbing the intense read-write bursts of synchronous checkpointing and reinforcement learning, so that your expensive accelerators remain fully saturated. To help organizations scale their workloads without breaking budgets, Managed Lustre’s new Dynamic Tier delivers more Lustre for less by consolidating hot and cold data into a single namespace, eliminating traditional caching performance cliffs. Finally, Managed Lustre Cloud Storage Mirror reduces the downtime and operational friction inherent in manual data transfers. Instead of you having to write custom scripts that leave expensive compute clusters waiting on files, it automatically synchronizes datasets in the background so they are ready before training begins. Proven in production at scale This purpose-built storage foundation is already powering customers’ most demanding AI workloads, helping them extract maximum return on investment from their compute resources. Thinking Machines Lab utilizes Cloud Storage Rapid Cache to stabilize read throughput peaks above 1.8 TB/s and achieve an 89% cache hit ratio, completely eradicating rate-limiting surge errors across their multi-region architecture. Shopify deployed 50+ unique Rapid Caches across their worldwide footprint, achieving over 2 TB/s peak throughput and up to a 90% latency reduction from their baseline to meet the data demands of their growing compute scale. Salesforce AI Research uses Managed Lustre as a high-throughput, low-latency external cache to keep their GPUs fully saturated, driving substantial performance gains for LLM inference over previous hardware generations. Atlassian adopted Managed Lustre on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to turn preemption interruptions into quick five-minute restores, delivering nearly 5x higher throughput and boosting their GPU utilization by 70% compared to NVMe-based systems. Harmonic relies on Managed Lustre to train mathematical reasoning models, eliminating 50% of experiment interruptions, cutting startup times in half, and increasing data retrieval speeds by 15x. The path forward When advising AI Infrastructure teams designing their stack today, our guidance is straightforward. First, evaluate your token economics rather than just legacy storage metrics. If your chips are waiting on data, optimizing storage is a cost-effective and efficient remedy. Second, avoid creating separate copies of data for every new workload; keep your primary data in a unified foundation and move it to the right tier as needed. Finally, while AI performance grabs the headlines, you can’t create your AI strategy on infrastructure built for a different era. At the same time, AI infrastructure needs enterprise-grade reliability, built-in security, and automated cost discipline for optimized TCO. The future of enterprise AI belongs to organizations that can turn their data into action. Google Cloud enables you to match the speed of your storage to the speed of your compute, so that you maximize your compute investments.
